messages.author: 0e3ac2129f920b6e
messages.subject: equating IRT models
parts:
Hello,
I am using mirt package for IRT models for sometime and I'm very happy with it. Now I need to equate some IRT models and I need some advice if it can be done in mirt as well. 
Thank you very much,
Amalia

messages.author: 0c672754339d5578
messages.subject: Re: equating IRT models
parts: Using multiple group IRT and concurrent calibration should provide the most rigorous linking of IRT scales across populations. This works with multiple test forms and across multiple population as long as each form is connected to other forms through link items, which can be complex connections or linkages. Fixed parameter linking is also possible. And in the worst case, parameters can be transformed to match certain targets such as averages of item difficulties and slopes from other forms. Common population linking is also straight forward.

Thanks Phil--

Say I have two datasets (using examples from simdata):


a <- matrix(rlnorm(30, .2, .3), 30)
d <- rnorm(30, mean = 0, sd = 1)

dataset1 <- mirt::simdata(a, d, 2000, itemtype = '2PL')
dataset2 <- mirt::simdata(a, d, 2000, itemtype = '2PL')


The last 10 items of dataset1 and the first 10 items of dataset2 are the same (anchor) items.  I want to fix the estimates from dataset1 Items_21-30 for the same items in dataset2.  How would I equate those?

Thanks!


Eugene

messages.author: 0c672754339d5578
messages.subject: Re: equating IRT models
parts:
Concurrent calibration with those items listed in the invariance statement is the most straightforward and defensible way of linking/equating IRT scales. 

Standard IRT equating (mean/mean Stocking Lord etc.) does not provide a model that incorporates true invariance assumptions, these weaker methods only exploit scale indeterminacy and do not constrain the model at all.

The invariance statement in the multiplegroup mirt call is pretty flexible, you can say which items are invariant, or what types of parameters, etc

see page 134 in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mirt/mirt.pdf

This equality constraint invariance modeling is standard and can be shown to be the strongest link (strict invariance on linking items) as for example described here: 
 
von Davier, M, Yamamoto, K., Shin, H.-J., Chen, H., Khorramdel, L., Weeks, J., Davis, S. Kong, N.  Kandathil, M. (2019) Evaluating item response theory linking and model fit for data from PISA 2000–2012, Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice, DOI: 10.1080/0969594X.2019.1586642

and here

von Davier, M., Khorramdel, L., He, Q., Shin, H. J., & Chen, H. (2019). Developments in Psychometric Population Models for Technology-Based Large-Scale Assessments: An Overview of Challenges and Opportunities. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 44(6), 671–705. https://doi.org/10.3102/1076998619881789

and here

von Davier, M. & von Davier, A. (2007). A Unified Approach to IRT Scale Linkage and Scale Transformations. Methodology, 3, 3, 115-124. https://econtent.hogrefe.com/ doi/abs/10.1027/1614-2241.3.3.115?journalCode=med

as well as

Xu, X. & von Davier, M. (2008). Linking with the General Diagnostic Model.  Research Report, RR-08-08. ETS: Princeton, NJ. http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/j.2333-8504.2008.tb02094.x/full

similar approaches that also allow partial invariance, just as the articles above, were described by  Glas & Jehangir, 2014, Glas & Verhelst, 1995, Yamamoto & Mazzeo, 1992, Oliveri & von Davier 2011.
